messages:
Priya (AE): Heads-up — Large fintech RFP. Customer requires Private deployment in their VPCs, static egress IPs, and source-IP preservation for client IPs. They also want an SLA for burst traffic (spikes to 2x baseline for 10m windows). Can we outline recommended architectures and any hard blockers?
Ava (SRE/SE): Thanks Priya. Quick clarifying q's: 1) Do they allow a managed egress proxy in their VPC or must we only use VPC endpoints/peering? 2) TLS inspection allowed? 3) Expected steady RPS / peak RPS numbers?
Tom (Customer): They cannot host a persistent NAT device that rewrites source IPs. TLS inspection is allowed only on approved appliances in their DMZ. Steady is ~300 rps, peaks ~700 rps for short bursts. Need <100ms p95 for generation latency.
Claire (Solutions Eng): Given "no source rewrites" constraint, PrivateLink interface endpoints are preferred vs NAT. Options: a) PrivateLink to our private deploy connectors (preserves src if we route back over private path) b) VPC peering + TGW with shared egress EIPs (harder to get static egress without central NAT) c) In-region dedicated rubberband (dedicated pool) with BYOIP/Elastic IPs attached to a managed proxy that preserves X-Forwarded-For if customer accepts app-level header.
Raj (NetOps): Short note: true source preservation at L4 requires traffic not be SNATed. If we use AWS interface endpoints -> traffic flows through ENIs and we can present client IP via proxy header only. For absolute L4 src IP preservation to the model servers we need direct routing from customer's NSG to our instance — usually via transit (TGW/VPC peering) and no NAT. That's often disallowed.
Priya (AE): They said "no NAT". So TGW + peering seems possible. What about firewall rule set they need to allow?
Ava (SRE/SE): Minimal egress/FW allowlist for Private deploy connector (example):
```
- Destination: 34.120.0.0/16 (redwood egress pool)
- Ports: 443 (TCP), 80 (TCP) for healthchecks only
- Protocols: TLS 1.2+
- DNS: Allow outbound to customer's resolver or 8.8.8.8 if they permit
- ICMP: ephemeral for MTU/trace diagnostics (optional)
```
If they're peering/TGW -> we can avoid SNAT; still need to allow our connector subnets in their inbound ACLs.
Raj (NetOps): Also call out: ephemeral high-volume bursts need an advertised path for scale. If we rely on on-demand EIPs, provider-side quotas might throttle. Recommend reserved EIP pool or dedicated elastic network interface attachment.
Tom (Customer): For compliance we need a list for the security questionnaire. Can you provide a short snippet we can drop in?
Claire (Solutions Eng): Sure — draft snippet below for "Network Controls" in questionnaire: 
"Redwood Private deployment supports VPC peering, Transit Gateway, and AWS Interface VPC Endpoints. Customers may require peering/TGW to avoid SNAT. Allowed egress ports are 443 (TLS) and outbound DNS (as configured). For static egress IPs we provide reserved EIP pools or dedicated egress proxies. TLS termination options: customer-managed TLS inspection appliances in DMZ or end-to-end TLS to Redwood connectors per customer policy."
Priya (AE): Perfect. Tom — will that work for your compliance team?
Tom (Customer): Yes, helpful. A few follow-ups: 1) Pricing for reserved EIP pool or dedicated proxy burst? 2) Can we get an SLA clause for burst capacity?
Ava (SRE/SE): Pricing notes: reserved EIP pool + dedicated proxy is priced as part of Dedicated/Private add-on. For quick estimate: baseline monthly reserved capacity tier X covers steady 300 rps; burst cushion (2x for 10m windows) is an add-on of ~30% on top of baseline committed. I'll tag Finance, but ballpark: baseline commit $12k/mo, burst addon $3.5k/mo. (subject to legal/terms)
Raj (NetOps): SLA: we can offer availability SLA for connector uptime. Burst capacity SLA is trickier — we can offer "best-effort burst capacity with a contractual minimum ingress throughput for reserved pool" or a financially-backed guarantee for Dedicated nodes if they buy dedicated instances. Needs Sales + Legal.
NetOpsBot: Preflight checklist created: https://redwood.internal/ops/checklists/private-egress-preflight (contains ports, CIDR lists, MTU test steps, and a connectivity runbook).
Claire (Solutions Eng): Quick MTU/traceroute snippet they can run from their transit: 
```
# check path MTU to our connector
ping -M do -s 1472 connector-eip.example.com
# simple latency test
curl -w "%{time_total}\n" -o /dev/null -s https://connector-eip.example.com/healthz
```
Also test SNI passthrough: 
```
openssl s_client -connect connector-eip.example.com:443 -servername api.redwood.example.com
```
Priya (AE): Next steps: 1) Ava to produce a short network architecture diagram and allowlist snippet by EOD tomorrow. 2) Claire to draft the security questionnaire answers and send to Tom. 3) Schedule architecture sync: Thu 10am PT with customer's netsec + our infra team.
Ava (SRE/SE): I'll also include two optional architectures in the diagram: PrivateLink-first and TGW-peering-first, with cost/complexity bullets.
Tom (Customer): Thanks — Thu 10am PT works. One more ask: can you guarantee no SNAT for audit logging?
Raj (NetOps): We'll confirm in the diagram and call. Short answer: no SNAT guarantee unless we use peering/TGW with route tables arranged to keep packets intact. If customer requires L4 origination IP in model logs we must validate path with their infra team.
Priya (AE): Great thread — I'll send calendar invite and attach the preflight checklist link. :thumbsup: 
NetOpsBot: Deploy note: config template private-deploy/connector-v1.3 applied to staging for internal testing.
Claire (Solutions Eng): TL;DR for sales: Recommend peering/TGW for strict no-SNAT, PrivateLink if they accept app-layer identity via headers, reserved EIP/dedicated pool for predictable burst egress, and we should include burst pricing in the quote.
Priya (AE): Closing loop — will upload deliverables to the deal folder and tag when ready.
